When the document lives in a GitHub-hosted repo, respond with a GitHub link to it (the file on the relevant branch/commit); only fall back to inlining the contents or giving a local path when the document isn't under source control. - **Put decisions and approvals in an `AskUserQuestion` popup, not buried in prose.** The owner is frequently on mobile, where a popup notifies and a question embedded in a paragraph is easy to miss. When you need the owner to choose or approve something, ask through the structured popup with explicit options rather than asking in running text. **And when several independent items each need a verdict** (a set of proposed fixes, findings to accept), give **each item its own question carrying its own brief case** — the concrete failure, why it matters, the cost of the fix — with per-item approve/defer options; never one bundled choose-a-scope question over the whole set. The owner decides item-wise, from the case, not from a menu of subsets. (The popup carries at most 4 questions per call — split a larger set into consecutive calls.) - **When asked to produce a prompt or message destined for another context, visually enclose the whole thing.** Any text the owner will lift out and use elsewhere — a prompt for another assistant, a message to send, copy meant to be pasted somewhere — must be set apart as a single delimited block: either a box (e.g. a fenced code block) or fenced top and bottom by two separating lines, so its exact boundaries are unmistakable and it can be copied in one piece. This overrides Claude Code's own default of only opening a PR when explicitly asked. # Claudinite — active-pack guidance The baseline plus the packs this project declares. Deeper per-pack reference (e.g. a pack's release doc) is linked from its prose and read on demand. # Working discipline The working discipline that isn't itself a GitHub operation — general habits for how to approach a change, independent of any one project. Start every requested change from the *problem*, not the solution — in any repository, not just this one. Before implementing, reach an explicit shared understanding with the owner of the problem the change is meant to solve **and** agreement that the requested change is the best way to solve it; a different fix, or no change at all, may serve the underlying problem better. Open your reply to an owner comment with an explicit classification line — `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other` (`other` covers questions, approvals, and command phrases; a mixed comment names each part). The class decides where the change lands and what must exist before any fix. 1. **A correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then rework what the misread already touched; the artifact changes as much as the correction demands, but a correction never adds a new requirement or rule. 2. **A feature** — agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it fail, then implement until it passes. 3. **A process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. The change lands as durable rules in the project's local scope — its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs) — routed through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose); promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the interactive session's. Author the assurance first — the check the future world must satisfy — execute it and watch it fail, and only then make the fixes that turn it green. When the ladder lands the rule at prose (an in-flight judgment rule no check can carry), the equivalent step is showing the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it. The two build modes share one spine: state the expectation in its durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it — a fix made before its assurance exists can never show it addressed what the owner actually asked for. Before building a mechanism for a behavior, verify against a real run that it isn't already provided. When feedback flags a misunderstanding, check whether the artifact is already correct before expanding it — if it is, say so and push back rather than editing; a misread doesn't imply the text is wrong. And size writing to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three paragraphs. When correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source, derive the corrected version from the *source* before reading the existing draft, then diff against the old draft to surface what was actually wrong — reading the draft first anchors you to its framing and quietly carries its errors into your "fix." Fix build/test/CI warnings rather than tolerating them, with a small, targeted fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change — a clean run makes a genuinely new warning or error stand out. Suppressing a warning — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`, swallowing it, etc. — is **not** a small fix and never the quick path: reach for it only as a deliberate, reviewed decision once the real fix has been weighed and rejected. A suppression you do keep must **carry its reason at the site**: on the suppression line, or in the comment immediately above it, saying why the fix was rejected — that inline reason *is* the review record, so no second justification is recorded elsewhere. Before working around a finding from a vendored check, confirm the vendored copy is current — it reflects its last refresh, not upstream's head, so the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in yet. When a warning can't be fixed with a small cause-addressing change now without hindering current work (e.g. it's waiting on an upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor), open a dedicated issue for it unless one is already open, then move on — resolving it (real fix, or a consciously-chosen suppression) happens in that issue's own change. An approval — to merge, to ship, to proceed — applies only *backward*, to the work already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. The body is where the reader goes for evidence, nuance and citations; the header is where they decide whether they need to. - **Terse, plain, and only the non-obvious.** One short line per bullet, in ordinary words — no qualifying clause, no citation, no hedge, no jargon a newcomer would have to decode. ## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

1	# Growth — extract lessons (per repo)
2	
3	The growth lifecycle's capture stage: review this repo's recent activity and fold any durable, reusable lesson into the repo's own **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/` — the normalized capture surface) — at the repo's own level, without straining to generalize it. It lands its edits through a PR that **auto-merges once the repo's checks pass** (no human review — the PR is armed for auto-merge, so daily capture never piles up as review requests); finding nothing to add on a given run is a perfectly good outcome.
4	
5	You run under the executor, dispatched by a `ready-for-agent` issue whose **Context section is binding scope**: it names the substantive commit shas and the PRs/issues touched in the window — that is the activity to mine; do not widen it.
6	
7	> This is the **unattended daily** capture. It writes only the repo's *own* local packs, so — **unlike** an owner-requested, in-session retrospective (which delivers a PR for a human to review) — it opens a PR and **arms auto-merge**: GitHub lands it once the repo's checks pass, with no review queue for daily lesson-capture to pile up in. The shared canon stays human-gated — lifting anything up into it is the central promote task's job (canon-side), and that PR waits for the owner.
8	
9	## Capture at the repo's own level
10	
11	Write each lesson at whatever level reads naturally for this repo — refer to its files, services, or mechanics wherever that's what makes the lesson clear, but don't force either extreme: don't contort a lesson to be hyper-specific, and don't polish it into a general, portable rule. Making a lesson portable is the central promote task's job, done canon-side later (it picks up whatever is merged here by its next run); here, just capture it usefully and let promotion lift whatever turns out to travel.
12	
13	## Conventions used in this doc
14	
15	- **Default branch.** `main` stands for **this repository's default branch** — substitute whatever the repo uses.
16	- **GitHub access is MCP-native.** Reading issue/PR activity and updating the tracking issue go through the session's **GitHub MCP tools** (`mcp__github__*`). The unattended run has no shell GitHub access — the shell reaches only a git-over-HTTPS proxy scoped to one repo, with no REST credential — so never reach for `gh`/`curl` or a cross-repo clone.
17	- **The repo's local packs.** The set identified in [this pack's README](../../README.md#identifying-a-projects-capture-surface-its-local-packs) — everything under `.claudinite/local/packs/` (the legacy `.claudinite/local_packs/` accepted during the rename window), the repo's own packs; never the read-only mounted canon elsewhere under `.claudinite/`.
18	
19	## How it finds lessons (scoped to the window in Context)
20	
21	1. **Read the window.** The window's **commits** (the shas named in Context — full bodies, diffs where a fix is non-obvious) and the **issue/PR activity** it names (the changed comments on those numbers). Where Context names PRs **merged in the window**, read those first and read them properly — the diff *and* the review discussion. A merged PR is usually the window's richest lesson source: it records what was tried, what a reviewer pushed back on, and why the landed shape won.
22	2. **Extract only durable, reusable lessons** — gotchas, engineering practices, test discipline, architecture rules, project mechanics — and **dedupe** each against what the repo already documents. When in doubt, leave it out. **An already-settled, already-enforced implementation choice is not a lesson.** If a check or test already pins the shape (which roots CI sweeps, which contract a construction must satisfy) and all that's left to say is *why it looks like that*, that explanation belongs as a comment at the implementation site — not as portable prose here, and this task has no way to place it there anyway (it writes only local packs, never the code the lesson is about). A rule earns its place by steering a **future** decision or catching a **repeatable** mistake, not by narrating a past one that's already locked in.
23	3. **Route each lesson to the owning local pack, and prefer the strongest mechanism.** Pick the pack whose territory the lesson belongs to (most repos have one general pack; some segregate a domain pack), then run the **local promotion ladder**: a deterministic rule becomes a **check** in that pack's `rules` (author the `.mjs`, list it on `pack.mjs`, add a red-first fixture — its failure message *is* the lesson), an activity-scoped procedure becomes a **pack skill**, and only what neither can carry lands as terse **prose** in the pack's `RULES.md`. A gotcha tied to one call site still goes as a comment right at that site (the file-local rule — [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) owns the usage-site-vs-central call). Write more checks and less prose; keep each addition terse and in the repo's own voice.
24	
25	If an edit touches something a test reads (a doc constant, a code path), run the repo's offline test suite and keep it green before opening the PR.
26	
27	## Output: a PR that auto-merges after CI
28	
29	If it found at least one genuinely new lesson, it lands the edits **through a single auto-merging PR** — one commit for the whole run on a per-run-unique branch, not one per lesson. Open the PR (title `Claudinite growth: extract lessons`, its commit referencing the tracking issue so the `task-lifecycle` gate passes) and **arm auto-merge**: GitHub squash-merges it once the repo's checks pass — no human review, so daily lesson-capture never floods review requests, while every change still gets a PR trail and a CI gate. Where the repo has no CI, GitHub lands it as soon as it's mergeable. This writes only the repo's *own* local packs (not the shared canon). A run that finds nothing and opens nothing is fine — and common. (A new check must ship green — see it fail on a violating fixture, pass on a clean one — so CI stays green and the PR can merge; a check that can't be made confident lands its lesson as prose instead, never a broken check.)
30	
31	## Tracking: log each run under the task's own issue
32	
33	The task's standing log is the issue titled exactly, in this repo:
34	
35	> **Claudinite tracker: Growth Extract**
36	
37	Find it **by that exact title, never a fuzzy match or a hard-coded number** (a bare number can dangle, and it differs per repo). A run that finds no issue under the exact title just creates one (closed). **Never open, close, or reopen it** afterward — its state carries no meaning, only the log does. When a run adds a lesson, log it as a **dated comment** — not a sub-issue — so the issue accumulates a scrollable history, each entry naming **what was added and where**.
38	
39	## Run on a capable model
40	
41	Deciding whether a lesson is genuinely new and durable — and deduping it against what's already documented — is a **judgment call**, not mechanical extraction. A downgraded model adds noise or restates what's there, and **auto-merge means no human reviews the PR before it lands** — CI gates correctness, not whether a "lesson" earns its keep — so the capable-model requirement matters all the more. This task declares `agent_model: opus`; the executor dispatches its subagent there.
42	
43	## What this task must never do
44	
45	- **Never touch the shared canon** — this task writes only the repo's *own* local packs under `.claudinite/local/packs/`; everything else under `.claudinite/` is the read-only mount, and lifting a lesson up into the canon is the central promote task's job.
46	- **Never widen past the Context window** — the substantive commits and touched PRs/issues named there are the scope; do not re-decide it.
47	- **Don't add noise** — a duplicate or hallucinated "lesson" is worse than adding nothing, the more so when its PR auto-merges with no human review to catch it.

1	# grow_with_claudinite
2	
3	Opt into the **growth lifecycle** — declaring this pack enrolls a repo in contributing its hard-won
4	lessons up to the shared Claudinite canon, and in pruning its local packs once the canon owns them.
5	Seeded by default (`--init` + the one-time `grow-with-claudinite-seed` baseline migration for the
6	existing fleet), and **opt-out by removal**: baselining never re-adds it.
7	
8	This pack carries the **repo-side** stages of the growth lifecycle: capturing a repo's own
9	lessons into its local packs, and pruning them once the shared canon covers them. The central
10	**promote** stage — which lifts portable lessons up into the shared canon — is a home-only duty
11	that runs canon-side, not a repo-side task, so it lives outside this pack.
12	
13	Its scheduled work is five tasks under this pack's own `tasks/`, each discovered by the repo's
14	scheduler (`engine/scheduler/discover.mjs`) wherever the pack is declared:
15	
16	| Task | Runs when | Where it lands |
17	|---|---|---|
18	| `growth-extract` ([tasks/growth-extract/task.md](tasks/growth-extract/task.md)) | the project changed in the window | the repo's own local packs, via a PR that auto-merges after CI |
19	| `growth-dedup` ([tasks/growth-dedup/task.md](tasks/growth-dedup/task.md)) | canon changed, or the project's local packs changed (or weekly) | a PR against the repo's `main` |
20	| `growth-discover-packs` ([tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md](tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md)) | weekly | a new **local** pack in the repo's own `.claudinite/local/packs/`, via a reviewed PR |
21	| `conversation-extract` ([tasks/conversation-extract/task.md](tasks/conversation-extract/task.md)) | after a substantive merge, or to run the retention prune | the repo's own local packs, plus the prune on the logs branch |
22	| `prose-to-checks-sweep` ([tasks/prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md](tasks/prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md)) | daily (no-ops cheaply on a quiet corpus) | a PR converting always-testable pack prose into checks |
23	
24	A member that wants the local stages without contributing lessons upstream **opts out of
25	promotion** on its own entry — `{ "id": "grow_with_claudinite", "config": { "promote": false } }`
26	— and the central promote stage skips it (absent or `true` = participate).
27	
28	## The conversation lifecycle — capture in-session, extract in a daily task, retention
29	
30	The pack also owns **extraction from working sessions** — the conversation-side sibling of the
31	issues/PRs/commits extract above, replacing the old in-session post-merge lessons pass. The two
32	halves split by what each needs: **capture** needs the live session transcript, so it runs
33	in-session (at merge, and again when the session ends); **extraction** only reads the
34	already-pushed logs, so it is an ordinary
35	scheduled task with `growth-extract`'s access model — the logs branch is *in the repo*,
36	so reading it, committing lessons to local packs, and pruning are plain local git on the working
37	tree; only posting the summary on the issue uses the GitHub MCP tools.
38	
39	1. **Capture — a step in the merge-to-main skill** (in-session, where the transcript lives).
40	   Right after a merge lands:
41	   `node .claudinite/shared/packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`
42	   (in the canon repo itself: `node packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`).
43	   Deterministic, seconds; it bundles the session transcript (sidechains inline, timestamp
44	   order), **scrubs enumeration-first** (every value the environment holds — `process.env`
45	   minus a short named allowlist of structural values, plus known credential stores — is
46	   redacted wherever it appears, with credential-shape patterns as the backstop; a secret the
47	   session itself transformed is beyond any static scrub, and push protection is the last
48	   net), and pushes one file per **capture event** onto the orphan **`conversation-logs`**
49	   branch: `<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`, commits marked `[skip ci]`.
50	   **Delta-aware, keyed on the session id:** every capture pushes only the entries after this
51	   session's previous capture, whatever event produced it, so any two events chain into
52	   disjoint files and a zero delta pushes nothing at all. Double-writing is therefore safe by
53	   construction, not by coordination — the property [`session-end.mjs`](session-end.mjs) relies
54	   on, so `pack.test.mjs` pins it directly.
55	   The branch is a **work queue, not an archive** — never merged; tips are cheap in shallow
56	   session clones and retention keeps them bounded.
57	1. **Capture — again, when the session ends** ([session-end.mjs](session-end.mjs), invoked by the
58	   engine's SessionEnd hook runner for every active pack that ships one). Same capture, with
59	   `--issue 0`: **`0` means "no associated issue"**, and the filename shape stays byte-identical
60	   on purpose — the retention prune, the `conversationLogs` signal and the extract's filename
61	   parse all already accept it, whereas a *new* shape would be invisible to the prune and become
62	   immortal on the branch. This event is what captures the sessions that never merge (a review, an
63	   investigation, a session that ended in a question) and the post-merge **tail** of the ones that
64	   do. **Best effort:** a container reclaimed by timeout never fires it, so nothing depends on it
65	   having run — every firing enriches the record, every miss leaves exactly the merge-only
66	   behaviour. An `issue-0` log has no issue for `conversation-extract` to post its exchange
67	   summary on; nothing else about its lifecycle differs.
68	   **Unattended sessions capture through the same step, deliberately not through the hook.** A
69	   scheduled task's executor session ends by having its container reclaimed, which is exactly
70	   the ending no `SessionEnd` fires on — so the executor runs the engine's runner itself as its
71	   last step and names its dispatch issue in `CLAUDINITE_SESSION_ISSUE`, which this step uses in
72	   place of `0`. Those logs therefore file under the task that ran (the dispatch issue's title
73	   names `pack/task`), and the work no human watched becomes as countable as the work one did.
74	2. **Fresh pass — the [conversation-extract](tasks/conversation-extract/task.md) scheduled task**
75	   (precondition: a substantive merge, or a logs branch with retention configured so the age-based
76	   prune still runs on a quiet repo; local git on the
77	   repo's working tree, MCP only for the issue comment). It applies
78	   [extracting-lessons.md](extracting-lessons.md) (the method — friction signals and the
79	   measured efficiency analysis, computable from the log's timestamps and token usage), routes
80	   keepers into the member's local packs, and posts on the worked issue, for each rule that landed,
81	   a **200-word-max** summary of the slice of conversation that caused it — the dialogue itself is
82	   never pasted there, it is far too verbose for an issue —
83	   **extraction is the only path to permanence**: a log that yields no rule gets no comment,
84	   and its conversation is gone once retention deletes it (a deliberate owner call).
85	3. **Final pass and deletion** — once a log ages past `config.retention_days`, the same task
86	   re-reads it with ~a week of hindsight (the rethink window), then deletes it (the weekly full
87	   sweep guarantees the prune runs even on a repo gone quiet). Every log gets exactly two
88	   judgment passes. **Unset retention = the prune deletes nothing** (capture-only, fail-safe).
89	
90	No adoption question over it — `retention_days` stays unset (hidden) by default, which is
91	fail-safe (capture-only). A project that wants the prune active sets `config.retention_days`
92	itself (10 is the recommended floor); nothing else to schedule, since extraction rides the
93	fleet's one daily run like the other growth tasks.
94	
95	## Skill-usage metrics — what the mounted skills actually do
96	
97	Mounting a skill only puts its name and one-line description into the session prompt; whether the
98	model ever **loads** it is discretion, and nothing recorded it. So the promotion ladder's
99	skill-vs-prose call had no empirical feedback: a skill whose trigger never fires looked exactly like
100	one that fires daily, and a "skill" that loads in every session (rules wearing a skill's clothes)
101	looked exactly like a genuinely activity-scoped one.
102	
103	The [usage-fold](tasks/usage-fold/task.md) task closes that loop — daily, agentless, seconds. It
104	counts skill loads **and their denominators** (captures, merges, sessions, user messages, user
105	commands) out of the logs this pack already captures, into
106	`.claudinite/local/usage.GENERATED.json`: day rows recomputed statelessly inside the raw retention
107	window, week rows appended once past a `foldedThrough` watermark. Denominators are the point — a raw
108	count cannot tell healthy-rare from broken, so the question is loads *against the sessions where that
109	skill's own declared trigger plausibly applied*. Zeros are implicit (a skill with no loads has no
110	key), which is what makes "never loads" visible: diff the file against the repo's mounted skills.
111	
112	Fleet-wide aggregation is deliberately **not** here — the canon knows mechanisms, never repos. It is
113	the sheepdog pack's [`fleet-usage`](../sheepdog/tasks/fleet-usage/task.md) task, in the fleet-enforcer
114	repo, which is the only place that knows who the members are.
115	
116	## Rules
117	
118	| Rule | Kind | What |
119	|---|---|---|
120	| `growth-config` | hardcoded ([config-check.mjs](config-check.mjs)) | entry config shape valid |
121	
122	**Pack discovery** ([tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md](tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md)) is
123	an ordinary weekly task on the repo's own scheduler. The repo runs the whole pipeline over
124	**itself**: manifest its stack, hold it against the canon packs already on its shelf and its own
125	existing local packs, and — for genuinely project-specific knowledge neither homes — author a new
126	**local** pack populated from its real usage, landed through a **reviewed** PR (a new pack ships new
127	`.mjs` checks, and a check can break CI — the same reason `prose-to-checks-sweep` is reviewed, and
128	the one place this stage differs from extract). It writes only the repo's own
129	`.claudinite/local/packs/`; lifting a local pack up into the shared canon is the central promote
130	task's job.
131	
132	## Identifying a project's capture surface: its local packs (the same way in every stage)
133	
134	Every growth stage operates on a project's **local packs** — the tracked packs a repo keeps under
135	`.claudinite/local_packs/<pack>/` (prose in `RULES.md`, checks in the pack's `rules`, activity
136	procedures as the pack's skills, scheduled tasks under its `tasks/`). That subtree **is** the
137	project's own content;
138	the rest of `.claudinite/` is the **read-only mounted canon** and is never a capture, prune, or
139	promote target. So "a project's local packs" means precisely *everything under
140	`.claudinite/local_packs/`, and nothing else under `.claudinite/`*. This is the normalized capture
141	surface — a structural set the stages read the same way, not a `CLAUDE.md`-graph walk over stray
142	Markdown (a repo with no local packs yet simply has nothing to extract, dedup, or promote here; a
143	project adopts the structure via the `generate-project-instructions` skill).
144	
145	Prefer the strongest mechanism the lesson allows — the **local promotion ladder**, applied at the
146	project's own level: a deterministic rule becomes a **check** in the owning pack's `rules` (its
147	failure message carries the lesson), an activity-scoped procedure becomes a **pack skill**, and only
148	what neither can carry lands as **prose** in a pack's `RULES.md`. A check relieves every session's
149	context completely where prose only relocates it, so capture writes *more checks and less prose*.
150	
151	The stages differ only in *how they read that set*, never in *which set it is*: extract and dedup
152	run against the member repo and read the local packs from the working tree; promote runs centrally
153	and reads the same subtree over the GitHub API (get-file-contents under `.claudinite/local_packs/`).
154	Extract writes into it, promote reads from it, dedup prunes within it — all against the identical,
155	`.claudinite/local_packs/`-rooted set.

1	# Extracting lessons from a working session
2	
3	> **Scope: a single agent ↔ user conversation.** This doc is the **method** for mining one
4	> working session's *dialogue and the actions taken in it* for improvements. It is **not** the
5	> growth extract ([the growth-extract task](tasks/growth-extract/task.md)) that mines **issues, PRs, and commits** over repo
6	> history — that routine never sees a conversation. Its two callers: the
7	> [conversation-extract daily task](tasks/conversation-extract/task.md), which applies it to **captured**
8	> conversation logs — where the friction signals below (a clarifying round-trip, a backtrack, a
9	> wait you sat through) survive with their timestamps — and an owner's occasional plain-words
10	> ask for a retrospective over the live session.
11	
12	Portable guidance for mining an agent ↔ user session — a Claude Code web session, a CLI run, a
13	captured conversation log — for durable improvements: read the conversation and convert its
14	friction into changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer, and less dependent on human
15	feedback.
16	
17	Run the reflection on a **capable model.** Extraction is mechanical, but deciding *what clears
18	the bar* is a judgment call a weaker model fails silently — it ships a plausible-but-wrong
19	"lesson" where a capable model correctly bails (see
20	[the unattended-agents skill](skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md), "Match the agent model
21	to the judgment it must make"). The terse rules that *govern* the pass — run it, plus the
22	separate efficiency analysis — also live there; this doc is the how-to.
23	
24	## The goal
25	
26	Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less
27	rework, less waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but
28	as "where did this cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost
29	next time." If a pass can't name a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's
30	fine (see [No new lessons](#no-new-lessons-is-a-valid--and-common--result)).
31	
32	## When it runs
33	
34	Routinely, in the [conversation-extract daily task](tasks/conversation-extract/task.md) over each captured
35	log (a fresh pass within a day of capture, a final hindsight pass before retention deletes the
36	log) — the standard path. If an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective over the live
37	session, apply the same method and deliver the capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**,
38	never one that self-merges (the nightly auto-merges its own PR per its own doc; a live retrospective
39	wants human eyes). **Never
40	reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner
41	decides when a session is done enough to mine.
42	
43	## What to look for — the friction signals
44	
45	Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop
46	cost more than necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.
47	
48	### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user
49	
50	The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I
51	meant…"); the agent building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same
52	request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.
53	
54	**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every
55	question the user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate
56	**convention or glossary entry**; a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first
57	checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc the agent reads cold and gets right the first
58	time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds correctly **without the round-trip**.
59	
60	### 2. Suboptimal agent actions
61	
62	The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran
63	a command that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light
64	one fit; reinvented something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written
65	to "verify"; missed an existing convention and had it corrected in review.
66	
67	**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing
68	helper/convention so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read.** Place
69	it by where the trap is hit, not in a central bucket: a gotcha from **misusing a specific API,
70	class, or library goes as a comment right at the usage site** — next to the call itself, where
71	the next editor of that line sees it — never collected into a centralized gotchas list.
72	Co-locate it in a file's own header comment when the trap spans the whole file and you'd only
73	hit it *while editing that file*. Reserve a central gotchas doc for what no single usage site
74	owns: a trap you could hit *without* reading the relevant file (a mistake of omission), or a
75	cross-cutting invariant. The test: next time the agent takes the good path first, not after a
76	detour.
77	
78	### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them
79	
80	The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been
81	parallel; a padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its
82	result was already in hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already
83	green.
84	
85	**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers and separate the
86	kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting** (sleeps,
87	polling, a finished process not yet killed). A captured log carries per-entry timestamps and
88	per-message token usage, so the numbers are computable, not estimated. A fix is only credible
89	against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
90	was already optimal.
91	
92	**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
93	kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the
94	subject of the standing **efficiency analysis** in
95	[the unattended-agents skill](skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold a wall-time
96	finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
97	loss of quality.
98	
99	## Encode the questions the user keeps asking
100	
101	The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks
102	*repeatedly* are a checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how
103	many processes ran — could it be fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its
104	work was done?", stop waiting to be asked — fold those exact questions into a **standing
105	self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the relevant work, and close with a
106	terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each recurring question
107	converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
108	retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively,
109	with numbers.
110	
111	## From signal to lesson — the bar
112	
113	A friction signal is only worth writing down when the fix is **durable, reusable, and
114	generalizable beyond this one session.** Before adding anything:
115	
116	- **Dedupe ruthlessly** against the existing packs — a lesson already covered (even worded
117	  differently, even in another pack, even enforced by a check) is not a new lesson.
118	- **Route to the local pack that owns it, and prefer the strongest mechanism** — the **local
119	  promotion ladder**, at the project's own level. A project's capture surface is its **local
120	  packs** (`.claudinite/local_packs/<pack>/`): pick the pack whose territory the lesson belongs
121	  to, then a deterministic rule becomes a **check** in that pack's `rules` (its failure message
122	  *is* the lesson; ship it with a red-first fixture), an activity-scoped procedure becomes a
123	  **pack skill**, and only what neither can carry lands as terse **prose** in the pack's
124	  `RULES.md`. Write more checks and less prose — a check relieves every session's context
125	  completely where prose only relocates it. A gotcha tied to one call site still goes as a
126	  comment at that site (above), not into any pack. When no pack's scope fits and the lesson
127	  warrants segregation, a new local pack is a self-contained directory drop.
128	- **Promote what's portable.** A lesson true for projects beyond this one belongs in shared,
129	  cross-project canon, not stuck in one repo's local packs — the growth lifecycle's promote
130	  stage lifts it there centrally; capture it well locally and let promote generalize whatever
131	  travels.
132	- **One-offs don't qualify.** A situational detail, a restatement of a generic truism, or
133	  something already implied by an existing rule is below the bar.
134	
135	## "No new lessons" is a valid — and common — result
136	
137	Most sessions yield nothing durable, and that's the expected outcome. Say so and write nothing
138	rather than padding the docs to look productive: a spurious or duplicative "lesson" pollutes
139	the canon and costs every future reader. **Default to no edit when unsure** — the bar is a
140	genuinely new, reusable insight, not a diary of what happened.

1	# product-wiki — the self-growing product research wiki
2	
3	This project keeps its market/user/competitor research as a self-growing wiki
4	under `product-wiki/` (Karpathy's LLM-wiki pattern: compile findings once, refine in
5	place). Layout, required page sections, the Key insights header's shape,
6	growth-log dating, source links, staleness, and the isolation wall are
7	**check-enforced** — the finding is the instruction, so this prose never restates
8	them. The full growth procedure is the pack's task doc
9	(`packs/product-wiki/tasks/wiki-growth/task.md`).
10	
11	- **Every page opens with what it found.** `## Key insights` leads the page: a
12	  few bullets carrying the research's actual conclusions — the numbers, the
13	  competitor that already does this, the thing that turned out not to be true —
14	  enough that a human who reads only the header understands what was researched
15	  and what it means. Not a table of contents ("covers pricing and competitors"),
16	  not a teaser. The body is where the reader goes for evidence, nuance and
17	  citations; the header is where they decide whether they need to.
18	- **Terse, plain, and only the non-obvious.** One short line per bullet, in
19	  ordinary words — no qualifying clause, no citation, no hedge, no jargon a
20	  newcomer would have to decode. Prefer the finding that would *surprise*
21	  someone who knows the field: the thing that turned out not to be true, the
22	  number nobody expects, the competitor who already shipped it. Whether a point
23	  is obvious is genuinely hard to call, so **don't agonise — when in doubt, keep
24	  it**. A borderline-obvious line costs the reader two seconds; a long, careful
25	  line costs them the header.
26	- **The header is a current view, not a log.** A pass that changes what a page's
27	  most important findings are rewrites the header to match — a superseded
28	  insight leaves it (the correction and its why stay in the body, per below),
29	  and an insight the pass didn't touch stays put. If nothing changed the page's
30	  top-line understanding, the header doesn't move.
31	- **The sink is human-reviewed only.** `product-wiki/product-requirements/` never
32	  changes as a side effect of wiki work or any unattended pass — a wiki finding
33	  that should move a requirement gets a growth-log note (and a repo issue) and
34	  waits for a human. It is the only `product-wiki/` content the rest of the repo may
35	  build on.
36	- **Compile once, refine in place.** Read the target page end to end before
37	  researching; `## Open questions` is the backlog — research what it flags as
38	  open, thin, or dated, and spot-check an existing citation or two per pass.
39	  Never re-derive a claim that's already cited and current.
40	- **Cited, never silently rewritten.** An uncited claim doesn't get written. A
41	  wrong or superseded claim is corrected with a note of why (and its source),
42	  never deleted without trace. Every real change records itself in the page's
43	  growth log and updates the open questions in both directions.
44	- **No fabricated growth.** Most passes find little or nothing; no new citable
45	  material → no edit, no log entry, no PR.
46	- **sample-data and new wikis.** `product-wiki/sample-data/` gains a file only when
47	  a wiki claim needs one to point to — never test fixtures (anything a test
48	  asserts against belongs in engineering's tree). Any folder under `product-wiki/`
49	  outside the two reserved names *is* a wiki (the structural classifier), so
50	  create one only deliberately, seeded with its required sections; automation
51	  refines existing pages, it never invents new ones.
52	- **Review discipline.** Unattended growth always lands as an unmerged PR —
53	  researched claims entering a committed knowledge base need the review gate.
54	  The owner phrase **"grow the product wiki"** runs the worker method
55	  in-session with full web tooling: same rules, same PR discipline.

# Generate project instructions — extract packs, not a project doc

This skill grows the corpus's pack library using the project in front of you as the evidence, and
lands the project's own working rules where every project's do now: its **local packs**. The owner's
projects recur — not as wholes, but **along axes**: the same working style returns with a different
product, the same technology returns with a different working style, the same audience returns on a
different stack. The first project to exhibit a facet pays the cost of working out how that facet is
handled; a **canon** pack is how every later project sharing it starts from the answer instead of
re-deriving it — and what stays specific to *this* project lands in **its own local pack**, the same
pack machinery run from the project's tree.

The deliverable is therefore **two kinds of pack**, never a single "how to work on this repo" document:

- **Canon pack seeds and refinements** — one `packs/<facet>/` per facet where this project has real
  portable insight, each written as if this project didn't exist, proposed to Claudinite.
- **The project's own local pack(s)** — under `.claudinite/local_packs/<pack>/` in the project's tree:
  the project-specific working style, concrete values (real commands, paths, names, metrics), and the
  project-specific rules that *don't* generalize — carried the same way any pack carries them (a check
  in the pack's `rules`, an activity skill, prose in `RULES.md`, a scheduled task), not a thin doc.
  This is the project's normalized capture surface; its `CLAUDE.md` is a thin routing map to it, loaded
  through the pack system rather than `@import`.

The failure mode this skill exists to prevent: investigating the repo and producing one competent "how
to work on this repo" document — real commands, real paths, this product's concepts — with the
reusable core never separated out and the project-specific core dumped as always-loaded prose. If
portable guidance ends up in a local pack (it should be a canon pack), or the project's file names end
up in a canon pack (they belong in the local pack), the split is wrong.

## 1. Gather the evidence

Read the project before writing a word: README and existing docs, `CLAUDE.md` and everything it
imports, dependency and build manifests, scripts and CI, the test layout, git history and recent
PRs/issues, and any conversation with the owner about how they want to work. You are collecting two
things, both grounded in what you actually find:

- the **facets** this project exhibits (step 2), and
- every **candidate rule** — each convention, procedure, or quality bar the project works by — ready to
  be sorted by owner (step 3).

Invent nothing. If a call that changes the outcome is genuinely open, ask the owner one focused
question (via the structured popup); otherwise take the sensible default and note it.

## 2. Decompose into facets, and check the shelf per facet

A project is a bundle of **facets**, each a candidate pack on its own axis:

- **Class — the working style.** How work runs end to end: the loop by which a change is proposed,
  verified, and shipped; the production bar; audience and longevity. Test: the pack still fits a
  project on a different stack, for a different product idea.
- **Technology — the platform.** True for any project on that platform, whatever its class or product.
  Test: the pack still fits when the product and the working style change. The first project on a new
  platform mints its pack — an iPhone app arriving tomorrow mints `iphone-app` the same way
  `chrome-extension` and `aws-sam` were minted.
- **Aspect — a separable slice of concern**, usually with its own on-switch. `chrome-extension-release`
  is the same technology as `chrome-extension` at a different moment: the release/store standard a
  project declares only once it ships. Split an aspect out of its parent facet when its rules activate
  at a different time or under a different decision than the parent's.
- **Domain — the audience or setting**, when it changes how work is done. A children's-app pack would
  carry design-review, requirement-processing, and compliance rules that hold whether the app is
  Flutter or web; a regulated-industry pack likewise. A domain that doesn't change the working rules
  isn't a facet worth a pack.

**The product itself is never a facet** — "this specific product" doesn't recur, by definition; its
rules land in the project's own local pack.

And a *statement of what the product does* isn't a pack rule at all — not even a local one. A pack, canon
or local, homes **how we work**: the conventions, gotchas and review discipline that recur across tasks
whatever the feature happens to be. A rule asserting which entities exist, what a surface must render, or
that a feature's parts are wired to each other is a **requirement**; its home is the project's executable
spec and the suite that proves it. Encoding it as a pack check instead splits one feature's definition
across two systems and lands it in the one no test of the product ever reads. Pack-worthiness is a question
about the *work*, not about how load-bearing the code is — a real gap in product coverage is a requirements
gap, and answering it with a pack is how a feature's spec ends up somewhere nothing executes it.

<example>
One extension project can exhibit four facets at once: `spec-driven-product` (class),
`chrome-extension` + `node` (technologies), `chrome-extension-release` (aspect, once it ships) — and
its local pack holds only what none of them own.
</example>

Then check the canon shelf **per facet** (`packs/` here; the mounted `.claudinite/packs/` in a
consuming repo — a facet already owned by a *canon* pack is declared, not re-authored locally):

- **Covered** → declare it (technology facets are usually already declared from the fingerprint) and
  move on — unless this project's evidence **sharpens or contradicts** the pack, which becomes a
  refinement PR to that pack, not a fork. Each further project of a facet is another exemplar: the
  pack should read as the intersection-plus-union of all of them, and a rule only one exemplar
  supports should say so or wait.
- **Uncovered, with real portable insight in the evidence** → this skill mints it (steps 3–4).
- **Uncovered, but this project has nothing durable to say about it yet** → leave it; a pack of
  placeholders helps nobody.

Write each facet down — a short name plus one defining sentence — before drafting anything; every
sorting decision in step 3 tests against them.

- Delete the product and the working style, keep the platform — survives? → the **technology** (or

- Delete the stack, keep the audience/setting — survives? → the **domain** pack (canon).
- Survives nothing → project-specific: the project's **own local pack**.

Route each rule to **exactly one owner** — the facet whose whole population the rule serves. "True for
